Green: neutral theory f x U x (G + 2 Ne) with the measured human mutation rate (1.25e-8 per site per generation): 12.2 M (8-21 M), observed/neutral = 1.4. Orange dashed: Mendel's Accountant's own neutral-class fixation rate (0.96 x Kimura in Rupe & Sanford's 300,000-generation runs) applied to the measured mutation rate; it lies on the green line. Orange markers: the model as published (Rupe & Sanford 2013, Table 1): 1,234-2,710 total and 79-1,476 'selective' fixations in 300,000 generations, obtained with 0.01 mutations per individual per generation, 7,100x below the measured rate; the arrow is that factor. Orange shading: with deleterious mutations included, the published human-parameter runs reach fitness 0 at generation 882 (no selection) or 40,831-83,647 (with selection), before the human-chimpanzee split time.

Eastern vs western gorilla. Blue: 0.30% (0.23-0.35%) pairwise SNV divergence (Scally et al. 2012: mean sequence divergence 1.75 Myr at 1e-9 per bp per year) = 4.4 M differences per lineage; population split 150 kyr-1.75 Myr, 19-year generations (8,000-92,000 generations). Green: neutral theory with the gorilla pedigree mutation rate, 2.5 M (1.2-5.4 M), observed/neutral = 1.7. Orange dashed: Mendel's Accountant's neutral-class fixation rate at the measured rate (on the green line). Orange markers at 300,000 generations: the model as published (0.01 mutations per individual per generation). The gorilla split lies inside the window in which the published runs with selection still have a surviving population (extinction at 40,831-83,647 generations), so here the fixation count is the test, and the model's own machinery at the measured mutation rate reproduces the observation within a factor of 2.

Modern humans vs Neanderthal (human-human). Blue: 31,389 SNVs fixed derived in 1,094 present-day humans and ancestral in the Altai Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes (Pruefer et al. 2014; a lower bound), split 550-765 kyr = 19,000-31,000 generations. Green: neutral theory with the fixation transient (f x U x G x fraction of fixations completed within G generations, Ne 7,000-15,000, from the Wright-Fisher fixation-time simulation in results/neutral_fixation_Q.json): 40,000, observed/neutral = 0.8. Orange dashed: Mendel's Accountant's neutral-class rate at the measured mutation rate, on the green line. The model's published extinction horizon with selection (40,831-83,647 generations) lies beyond the Neanderthal split, so the fixation count is the test here too, and it matches.

Experiment 0 from the model's published numbers. Green: Wright-Fisher expectation for cumulative neutral fixations per unit gametic mutation rate, U x G x Q(G), where Q is the fraction of eventual fixations completed within G generations (simulated, mean fixation time 3.97 N; results/neutral_fixation_Q.json), for N = 100, 1,000, 10,000. Dashed: Kimura's k = U. Orange: Rupe & Sanford 2013 Table 1 all-neutral runs, 1,413 (N = 1,000) and 1,234 (N = 10,000) fixations in 300,000 generations at a gametic rate of 0.005, i.e. 0.95-0.96 of the Kimura expectation with the transient. The 'waiting time to fixation rate equilibrium' they describe is the standard 4N transient: at 13,500 generations a population of 10,000 has completed 2.5% of its eventual fixations.

The model's published fitness trajectories for human-like parameters (orange; Sanford et al. 2008: 10 mutations per individual and no selection, fitness 0 at generation 882; Gibson et al. 2013: default DFE with 5 deleterious mutations per individual, partial truncation, h2 = 0.4: 0.79-0.84 at 10,000 generations and fitness 0 at 40,831; Lynch's DFE with 3 deleterious mutations per individual: 0.31 at 100,000 or fitness 0 at 83,647; with 12 offspring per female 0.22-0.57 at 10,000; only published endpoints are drawn, paths are interpolated). Green: standard model, constant mean fitness at mutation-selection balance. Grey dashed: Lynch 2016, 0.1-0.5% decline per generation IF selection were completely relaxed. Blue: generations since the Neanderthal-modern human (24,000), eastern-western gorilla (26,000; 8,000-92,000) and human-chimpanzee (252,000; 190,000-375,000) splits, all of which the lineages survived.

Experiment 0, own Mendel's Accountant runs (mendel-go 1.2.5 compiled from source). One neutral mutation per individual per generation, no selection, populations of 100, 300 and 1,000 for 20 N, 20 N and 8 N generations; orange = neutral alleles at 99-100% frequency (cumulative fixations) read from the allele-bin files every 100-200 generations. Dashed green = Wright-Fisher expectation U x G x Q(G/N) with Ne = N; solid green = the same with Ne fitted (1.29 N, 1.09 N, 1.27 N), consistent with the 1.33 N expected from the simulator's fixed-offspring-number mating (each pair has exactly 4 offspring, half culled at random). With that Ne the runs follow Kimura's k = U to within 5%: final counts 738 / 2,443 / 1,576 against 736 / 2,324 / 1,615 expected.

Experiment 1: the model as published, re-run in mendel-go. Sanford et al. 2008 default human run (N = 1,000; 10 mutations per individual, 9:1 deleterious:beneficial; Weibull DFE with 0.1% of effects > 0.1; co-dominant; probability selection; heritability 0.2; 6 offspring per female). Left: mean fitness; right: mutations per individual (orange deleterious, blue beneficial) with the published generation-1,000 values as squares: 8,822 vs 8,730 deleterious and 970 vs 1,011 beneficial, so the published run reproduces. The published 'fitness 0 at generation 882 without selection' does not: mendel-go removes individuals whose additive fitness reaches zero, which with no surplus collapses the population by bookkeeping (not shown) and with random survival acts as truncation at zero (dotted: 0.36 at 882, levelling near 0.3). The 10,000-generation run (dashed) reached fitness 0.418 with 24,468 deleterious and 2,800 beneficial alleles fixed (published 16,116 and 3,193); the total, 27,268, is 1.13 x the neutral expectation for the gametic mutation rate of 5, i.e. in the model deleterious mutations fix at the neutral rate when every mutation is tracked.

Experiment 2: Mendel's Accountant with 70 new mutations per individual per generation (the measured human rate), N = 1,000, varying one assumption at a time from a base case (5 of the 70 deleterious with Sanford's default DFE, probability selection, heritability 0.2, beneficial fraction 1e-4). Left: mean fitness; right: accumulated deleterious mutations per individual. Base: 0.64 at 10,000 generations, 0.47 at 20,000, 0.41 at the Neanderthal split (24,074) and 0.395 at 25,000: a decelerating decline of 2-4e-5 per generation (not 1-2%), extrapolating to zero near generation 42,000. Declaring all 70 mutations deleterious (dotted) collapses the population by generation 7,124. The high-impact DFE Gibson et al. used for Lynch's estimate (dashed, U_del = 2) declines faster than the base despite fewer deleterious mutations. Full truncation selection (brown) removes the load almost entirely (0.993 at 10,000); partial truncation 0.84. Heritability 1.0 and beneficial fractions of 1e-3 or 1e-2 are indistinguishable from the base; a tenfold larger population (N = 10,000, purple) slows the decline modestly (0.72 vs 0.64 at 10,000 generations). The decline is therefore set by how many mutations are declared deleterious and how large their effects are, by the additive combination of effects, and by the selection mode; not by noise or by beneficial mutations.

Experiment 3 (reduced): LTEE-like inputs in Mendel's Accountant. The program has no haploid or clonal mode, so this is a diploid population of 1,000 without crossover, genome 4.63e6, Sanford's DFE, probability selection, 60,000 generations, at the LTEE's ancestral (4.1e-4) and 100x mutator (0.041 per genome per generation) mutation rates, with the model's default (1e-4) or a generous (1e-2) beneficial fraction and maximum beneficial gain 0.1. Orange: model fitness, 0.955-0.966 at 60,000 generations for the mutator rate (3.5-4.5% decline, 1,032-1,140 deleterious and 0-4 beneficial fixations) and 1.000 for the ancestral rate. Blue: the observed LTEE grand mean, relative fitness ~1.7 after 50,000 generations (Lenski 2017, quoting Wiser et al. 2013). The model's beneficial-mutation assumptions cannot produce the adaptation that is the experiment's main result.

Experiment 2b: the same inputs in a free-recombination Wright-Fisher simulator (N = 1,000, no noise) with mutation effects combined additively (solid; what Mendel's Accountant does) or multiplicatively (dashed; standard population genetics). Sanford's DFE with 5 deleterious mutations per individual (orange): 0.594 vs 0.592 at 10,000 generations, and 0.640 in Mendel's Accountant itself; the combination rule does not matter. All 70 mutations deleterious (brown): 0.044 additive at 10,000, 0.023 multiplicative at 3,000. A gamma DFE (shape 0.19, mean 0.01, approximate) with 2 deleterious per individual (green): 0.348 vs 0.177. The decline is set by the DFE's mass below the selection threshold (about 18% of Sanford's mutations have effects between 1e-6 and 1e-4 and accumulate at the neutral rate), i.e. by the assumption that unconstrained sites are slightly deleterious rather than neutral.
